name: Growth-plate peptides (IGF-1/MK-677 for height)

card.summary: Growth hormone secretagogues like MK-677 (and IGF-1 products) pitched as a way to gain height; trials exist only in children with growth hormone deficiency, none in healthy short people.
card.aka: MK-677, ibutamoren, LUM-201, GH secretagogues, heightmaxxing peptides
card.note: MK-677 is an unapproved investigational drug, and no trials have tested it for height in healthy short individuals.

quick.overview:
This entry covers the practice of using growth hormone (GH) boosting compounds, most often the oral drug MK-677 (ibutamoren) and sometimes IGF-1 products, in an attempt to grow taller before the growth plates close. It sits within the wider height discourse in looksmaxxing communities.

Published research on these compounds is in children and adults with diagnosed growth hormone deficiency or in older adults, not in healthy people who are simply short. Comparisons of GH treatments in deficient children measure height velocity and IGF-1 levels, and a Phase 3 trial of LUM-201 (the pharmaceutical name for ibutamoren) in children with GH deficiency is registered.
quick.mechanism: MK-677 mimics ghrelin at the ghrelin receptor and raises GH and IGF-1 levels, which are the hormones that drive growth in childhood. In growth hormone deficiency, injected GH is the standard therapy and is reported to add roughly 5 to 10 cm to predicted adult height in treated short-stature children.
quick.risks: MK-677 is an Investigational New Drug and not approved for marketing in the US. Adult studies describe raised cortisol alongside raised GH and IGF-1. No published trial tests these compounds for height in healthy people, and growth plate closure limits any growth window after puberty.

lead: Growth-plate peptides is a looksmaxxing term for growth hormone (GH) secretagogues and related products, chiefly MK-677 (ibutamoren) and IGF-1, used with the aim of gaining height. The idea is a chain: raise GH and IGF-1 while the growth plates are still open, stimulate cartilage growth at the ends of the long bones, and end up with a taller adult frame.[1][8] Height is among the most discussed measurements in appearance culture, and communities devoted to it treat the teen years as a window in which growth might be influenced.[12][14]

MK-677 is an orally active, non-peptide ghrelin receptor agonist originally developed by Merck. It raises GH and IGF-1 for about a day after a single dose and also raises cortisol.[1] Forum users group it with injectable GH and IGF-1 variants under the label of height peptides, even though it is a small molecule.[1][12]

Published research on GH-axis drugs for height concerns children with diagnosed growth hormone deficiency, children born small for gestational age and some syndromic conditions. A 2026 meta-analysis compared once-weekly somatrogon with daily somatropin in prepubertal children with GH deficiency,[2] and a Phase 3 trial of LUM-201, the pharmaceutical name for ibutamoren, in children with GH deficiency is registered.[3] Controlled studies of MK-677 itself are mostly in older adults and adults with GH deficiency, where it raised GH and IGF-1, increased fat-free mass and altered markers of bone turnover.[16][17][20] Reviews note that the only paediatric ibutamoren trials measured hormone levels or growth velocity in GH-deficient children rather than adult height, and no published trial has tested these compounds for height in healthy short individuals.[18][19]

Medical short stature is usually defined as adult height more than two standard deviations below the population mean. GH therapy in treated children is reported to add roughly 5 to 10 cm to predicted adult height, at high cost and over years of daily or weekly injections.[4][7]

chain: Ghrelin-receptor agonist or IGF-1 product raises GH/IGF-1 signalling
Growth-plate cartilage continues to lengthen the long bones while the plates remain open
Taller adult height (the aim as described by users)
angle.text: People in height communities use MK-677 and IGF-1 products hoping to extend or accelerate long-bone growth before the plates fuse, usually in the teens or early twenties. Clinical GH therapy is documented to add centimetres in deficient children, but the oral secretagogue route has been studied in deficient children and adults rather than in healthy people seeking height.

paras: The practice centres on the idea that raising GH and IGF-1 during or near the end of puberty could lengthen long bones before the growth plates fuse. In community usage the products are grouped as peptides or secretagogues, although MK-677 is a non-peptide small molecule.[1] Three families of products recur in discussion: oral ghrelin-receptor agonists such as MK-677; injectable GH, which is a prescription medicine; and IGF-1 itself, the growth factor through which much of GH's effect on bone is mediated.[8][7]

Ibutamoren was developed as MK-677 (L-163,191) at Merck, with early design work described in a 1995 paper, and has since been associated with Lumos Pharma as LUM-201. A former tentative brand name was Oratrope.[1][19][21] It belongs to a class of GH-releasing peptide mimetics: compounds that act at the ghrelin (GH secretagogue) receptor to prompt the pituitary to release its own GH in pulses, rather than supplying GH from outside.[18][21]

Related ideas discussed alongside it on looksmax.org include so-called IGF-1 signalling through diet, such as sugar intake or supplements like chromium, which proponents say supports bone growth; these are described under the claims below.[9][10]

The epiphyseal plate, or growth plate, is a layer of cartilage near each end of a long bone. Cartilage cells there divide and stack, then are replaced by bone, which lengthens the bone. Rising oestrogen in puberty in both sexes increases the death of these cells until the cartilage is fully replaced by bone and a thin line remains.[8]

Fusion is reported to finish as early as about 12 in females and 14 in males, with most occurring around 14 to 15 and 15 to 17 respectively; one study of the lower leg bones found complete fusion in all females by 18 and all males by 19.[8] This is why height-focused communities frame the topic around a time window in the teens.[8][14]

Ibutamoren mimics the body's own hormone ghrelin, increasing secretion of GH and IGF-1 and keeping IGF-1 elevated for up to about 24 hours after a dose. It also raises cortisol.[1] A 2017 review gives oral bioavailability above 60 percent and a half-life of about 4.7 hours in humans; in beagles the elimination half-life is reported as 4 to 6 hours.[18][1]

In a randomised, placebo-controlled study of 32 healthy people aged 64 to 81, two weeks of MK-677 increased mean 24-hour GH concentrations in a dose-dependent way by enhancing existing pulses of secretion, and raised IGF-1 into the range seen in young adults.[16] The same study recorded rises in fasting glucose and reductions in insulin sensitivity.[16]

In adults, studies reported increases in lean body mass without changes in total fat mass, and higher bone turnover markers, prompting interest in frailty in older people.[1][17][20] A small study of 14 subjects found that a bedtime dose increased REM sleep by about 20% in young and 50% in older subjects, and increased slow-wave sleep by about 50% in young subjects.[1]

No studies in healthy short people were found. Research related to this topic is limited to patients with diagnosed deficiency, small-for-gestational-age children and older adults. A 2021 commentary on oral secretagogues in paediatric GH deficiency describes two six-month studies in GH-deficient children in which mean annualised growth velocity was 6.0 and 6.9 cm per year on oral LUM-201, versus 4.5 cm per year on placebo and 11.1 cm per year on injected GH; the authors note that bone-age effects and long-term safety remain to be studied and suggest children with normal GH responses may be the best candidates.[19] Wikipedia reports that Phase 2 trials of LUM-201 in paediatric GH deficiency met their primary and secondary endpoints.[1] A Phase 3 study of LUM-201 in 150 children with GH deficiency began recruiting in May 2026.[3]

A systematic review of seven studies compared weekly somatrogon with daily somatropin in prepubertal GH-deficient children and found greater IGF-1 SDS increases with somatrogon but no significant difference in height SDS change.[2] A long-term multicentre observational study in children born small for gestational age reported that GH treatment improved height without leading to insulin resistance or an excessive IGF-1 rise over about 10 years.[5]

For injectable GH in short children without deficiency, trials in extreme idiopathic short stature with about four years of treatment gained roughly 4 to 8 cm in adult height, and Turner syndrome gains were about 5 to 8 cm.[7] A 2017 review of secretagogues reports small studies of other secretagogues in short children, including one in which growth velocity rose from 5.3 to 8.3 cm per year in eight prepubertal children given intranasal hexarelin, and notes that ibutamoren had one paediatric trial measuring GH and IGF-1 over seven days without growth rates.[18]

In 1996 Chapman and colleagues reported a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 32 healthy older adults aged 64 to 81 showing that daily oral MK-677 stimulated the GH-IGF-1 axis.[16] A separate study in nine severely GH-deficient young men found that MK-677 raised IGF-1 and 24-hour GH, and was generally well tolerated over four days.[22]

A pooled analysis of three placebo-controlled studies in 187 older adults found increases in IGF-1 of 55 to 94 percent and rises in bone formation and resorption markers.[20] In a 2008 two-year placebo-controlled trial in 65 healthy adults aged 60 to 81, MK-677 raised GH and IGF-1 to young-adult levels and fat-free mass rose by about 1.1 kg versus a 0.5 kg fall on placebo; visceral and total fat did not differ significantly.[17] An 18-month trial in 292 postmenopausal women examined MK-677 with and without alendronate on bone markers and density.[23]

Recombinant IGF-1 (mecasermin, brand name Increlex) is a prescription injection indicated in the US, Canada and Australia for growth failure in children with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency, such as Laron syndrome (GH insensitivity).[24] Community posts that refer to IGF-1 for height usually mean this class or the dietary and supplement routes below, rather than a formulation available without a prescription.[9][10][24]

Ibutamoren is an Investigational New Drug and has not been approved for marketing in the United States. It has been used experimentally in bodybuilding and is banned in most sports.[1] A review of doping endocrinology covers GH, GH-releasing peptides and IGF-1 as substances prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency and discusses their side effects and detection.[11]

A 2017 review of secretagogue safety reports that a hip-fracture trial of MK-677 was stopped early over concerns about congestive heart failure (6.5 percent on drug versus 1.7 percent on placebo), that adverse events overall were more frequent on the drug (77 versus 55 percent), and that hyperglycaemia and reduced insulin sensitivity were the most consistent concerns. Increased appetite, musculoskeletal pain, fluid retention and transient rises in cortisol and prolactin were also reported, and the authors noted no safety data on malignancy or mortality.[18]

For GH therapy, the literature notes that GH usually lowers insulin sensitivity, that a large study found no overall rise in cancer risk but elevated risk in some subgroups, and that the FDA's 2011 review of mortality risk was inconclusive.[7] Costs for a small child on GH are roughly US$20,000 a year.[4] Gray-market products sold online as research chemicals are not subject to the quality testing of approved drugs.

Growth hormone releasing peptide was discovered in 1981, and orally active peptide mimetics were later developed, including Merck's MK-677; a 1997 Merck review in Endocrine Reviews describes the design of these peptidomimetics.[25][21] Chapman's trials of MK-677 in older and GH-deficient adults were published in 1996 and 1997.[16][22]

Pituitary-derived GH was used for children from the late 1950s until 1985, when cases of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in recipients ended its use and the FDA approved Genentech's recombinant GH, Protropin.[7] Approval of GH for idiopathic short stature (Humatrope, 2003) is described as controversial among clinicians because it treats very short stature with normal GH tests as a condition to be treated, and was followed by more parents seeking GH for non-deficient children.[7]
Ibutamoren was listed as preclinical for GH deficiency in 2017, later reached Phase 2 and Phase 3 paediatric development as LUM-201, and the Phase 3 trial registered in 2026.[1][3]

Height is a central topic in looksmaxxing communities, and discussions of MK-677 on looksmax.org include threads by teenage users asking about use at 14 and 16, questions about sourcing and appetite, and comparisons of MK-677 with injectable GH.[12][14] Gym and bodybuilding forums such as T Nation host separate threads on MK-677 for physique use, where users report appetite and body-composition changes.[13]

Other posts in the same communities discuss non-pharmaceutical routes said to support IGF-1 signalling, including carbohydrate intake and chromium; one thread asks whether such 'IGF-1 signaling' is real or a coping story, with some users sceptical of the idea.[9][10]

timeline.event: Growth hormone releasing peptide is discovered; orally active mimetics follow in later decades.[25]
The FDA approves recombinant GH (Protropin) after cadaver-derived GH is withdrawn over Creutzfeldt-Jakob cases.[7]
Early design work on the MK-677 compound is described in a paper.[1][19]
Randomised trial of oral MK-677 in 32 healthy older adults reports GH-IGF-1 axis stimulation.[16]
FDA approves Humatrope for idiopathic short stature.[7]
Two-year randomised trial in 65 older adults reports fat-free mass gain with MK-677.[17]
Ibutamoren is listed as in the preclinical stage for GH deficiency; a review of secretagogue safety is published.[1][18]
Commentary reviews oral secretagogue trials in paediatric GH deficiency.[19]
A Phase 3 trial of LUM-201 in children with GH deficiency begins recruiting in May.[3]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, MK-677 and IGF-1 come up in threads about bone growth and heightmaxxing, with views ranging from enthusiasm to open scepticism among users themselves.[12]

claims.claim: MK-677 can add height or bone growth before the plates close
claims.believers: Users post threads about MK-677 for better bone growth and about use in the mid-teens, reasoning that raising GH and IGF-1 stimulates growth.[14]
claims.experts: MK-677 has been studied for GH and IGF-1 levels in deficient children and adults, not for height in healthy short people; no published trial has tested it for that purpose.[1][3]

claims.claim: Dietary 'IGF-1 signalling', including a high sugar intake, increases bone growth and height
claims.believers: One looksmax.org reply suggests a very high daily sugar intake to increase bone mass and height, while a related thread asks whether IGF-1 signalling is real or a coping story, with some users sceptical.[9][10]
claims.experts: Reviews describe diet and glycaemic load as influencing IGF-1 and insulin in relation to acne, rather than as a height intervention.[15]

claims.claim: Chromium supplements raise IGF-1 enough to accelerate bone growth
claims.believers: A forum post cites studies on chromium and insulin sensitivity and animal muscle-cell IGF-1 mRNA to argue chromium could raise IGF-1.[9]
claims.experts: The research cited in the post concerns insulin sensitivity and cell or animal models; no published human trial has tested chromium for height gain.

claims.claim: Injectable GH is the strongest route to height compared with MK-677
claims.believers: Forum threads compare MK-677 against injectable GH and describe peptide users arguing over which is superior.[12]
claims.experts: GH therapy is documented to add centimetres in treated deficient children and some other groups, under medical supervision, with ongoing monitoring of metabolic effects.[4][7]

claims.claim: MK-677 is a safe, convenient alternative to injected GH
claims.believers: Posters describe an oral product that avoids needles and gives appetite and sleep effects as bonuses.[12][13]
claims.experts: Reviews report hyperglycaemia, reduced insulin sensitivity, fluid retention and appetite increase, and a hip-fracture trial was stopped early over heart-failure concerns.[18]

claims.claim: Growth plates keep a 'window' open so GH-axis products can still add height in the late teens
claims.believers: Teenage users ask whether use at 16 or later can still matter, treating plate status as the deciding factor.[14][12]
claims.experts: Fusion is reported to complete around 14 to 17 years on average, with one study finding all females fused by 18 and all males by 19; no trial tests MK-677 on healthy teens.[8][3]
